::: {.why}
Trading rounds test whether you compute an expectation quickly and whether you notice when the expectation is negative, and the second failure is the one that ends interviews.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Answer eight expected value questions in twenty minutes, including at least one you should decline.
- State the two-part answer format: the number, and the assumption it rests on.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Twenty minutes, eight questions, out loud. Use the two-part format every time: the expected value, then the one assumption that would change it. Interviewers ask about the assumption, so volunteering it saves a round trip and shows you know where the answer is fragile.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Then the harder skill: for each question, say what you would pay and what you would sell at, which is a width around the expectation rather than the expectation itself. That conversion from an estimate to a two-sided market is the actual job and it is what the round is testing.
:::
:::

I offer you a game with an expected value of plus two dollars and a variance of a thousand. Do you play, and how much?
:::
